title: Practice: units of measurement
intro: Eight questions, finishing with a timed conversion drill.

hints: A microsecond is bigger than a nanosecond, so the number should get smaller.
questions.explanation: $34\,000 \div 1000 = 34\ \mu\text{s}$. The number got smaller because we moved to a larger unit.

hints: A megabyte is smaller than a gigabyte, so the number gets bigger.
Micro is one step smaller than milli, so multiply by 1000.
Kilo to mega is one step up; mega to giga is another.
Two steps up means dividing by $1\,000\,000$.

questions.prompt: Put these units in order, **smallest first**.
hints: Nano, micro and milli are all smaller than a metre.
Each step is a factor of 1000.
questions.explanation: nano $<$ micro $<$ milli $<$ base $<$ kilo $<$ mega, each a thousand times the last.

questions.prompt: Match each prefix to its power of ten.
hints: Negative powers are the small ones; positive powers are the large ones.
questions.explanation: nano $=10^{-9}$, milli $=10^{-3}$, kilo $=10^{3}$, giga $=10^{9}$. Notice nano and giga are mirror images either side of the base unit.

questions.prompt: Which is the most sensible unit for the thickness of a sheet of paper?
hints: All four are the same measurement — the question is which is easiest to read.
A good unit gives a number that is easy to say.
questions.explanation: All four are equal. $0.1\ \text{mm}$ is the clearest for everyday use, though $100\ \mu\text{m}$ is a perfectly good scientific alternative. $0.0000001\ \text{km}$ is correct but nobody would write it.

questions.prompt: Quick-fire: unit conversions. Give numbers only.
questions.explanation: Every one is a multiplication or division by a power of 1000 (or 100 for cm). Before answering, decide whether the number should grow or shrink — that alone gets most of them right.
